opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think what's interesting about O1 is that it's a step in a direction I've been talking about for a long time, which is moving beyond pure pattern recall from a single forward pass of a model toward some form of test-time search. With O1, the model generates natural-language chains of thought, and those chains can be read as a kind of program, a sequence of steps meant to solve a specific problem. During training it was taught to explore the space of possible chains and to find the ones that lead to correct answers. So you could say it's doing a form of search over a space of programs, where the programs are written in natural language rather than in some formal DSL.

That's a meaningful change. It's no longer just "fetch the template that matches this prompt and apply it." It's recombining things at inference time to adapt to the problem at hand, and that's a big part of why it does much better on tasks that need genuine novelty, including ARC-style tasks.

But I'd add some important caveats. First, the search is fundamentally guided by the model's intuition, its learned prior over which steps look promising, and there's no strong verification step. In a classical program synthesis system you can execute the candidate program and check whether it produces the right output. With a natural-language chain of thought you can't really execute it; you only have the model's own judgment about whether it looks right. So errors compound, and you can't trust the output the way you'd trust a verified program.

Second, it's very expensive. You're spending a lot of compute exploring this space, and the efficiency of that search is still far from what humans do. When you or I face a novel puzzle, we don't try thousands of chains of thought. We have a very strong intuition that narrows the space to a handful of candidates, and then we check them deliberately.

So where I think this goes is a real merger of the two paradigms. You use deep learning for what it's good at: intuition, perception, and guiding the search by telling you which branches look promising. You use discrete program search for what it's good at: composing building blocks into something genuinely new and verifying that it works. Deep learning provides the System 1 that makes search tractable, and the discrete program representation provides the System 2 that gives you generalization and reliability. O1 is an early, rather crude version of that. The models that really crack fluid intelligence will be much more explicit about it, with an actual library of reusable abstractions that grows over time, a search process guided by learned intuition, and a way to check candidate solutions against reality.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think O1 is actually a genuine breakthrough in terms of how much generalization power you can get out of these systems, and the way I'd describe it is that it's doing something like program synthesis, but in the space of natural language instructions rather than in the space of code.

The way it works, as far as we can tell, is that it's running a search process at inference time. It generates many candidate chains of thought, it evaluates them, it backtracks, it branches, and it's doing this in natural language. And a chain of thought, if you think about it, is really a program. It's a sequence of steps that describes how to go from the problem to the solution. So when O1 is searching over chains of thought, it's searching over a space of natural language programs, and then it's executing those programs using the LLM itself as the interpreter.

That's a very big departure from the classical LLM paradigm, which is pure memorization and retrieval. In a classical LLM, you prompt the model and it fetches a program that it's memorized from its training data, and it applies it. There's no adaptation happening at test time. What O1 adds is test-time adaptation. It's recombining the building blocks it's learned into something new, on the fly, to fit the specific problem in front of it. And that's exactly what I've been arguing is necessary for intelligence: the ability to synthesize new programs when you face a situation you haven't seen before.

Now, there are limitations. The search is happening in a space that's still bounded by what the model has memorized, so the building blocks are fixed, and the search process itself is fairly inefficient. It's using a lot of compute. If you look at ARC, for instance, the base models score near zero, and O1-preview is somewhere around twenty percent with a basic prompting setup, which is a real improvement, but it's still far from what a human child can do with almost no compute at all. So the search is doing real work, but it's not yet a very efficient search, and the model doesn't have a way to learn from the results and consolidate them into reusable abstractions. That's the next step. You want the system to not only synthesize a program at test time, but to add that program back into its library so that the next search is cheaper. That's how you get something that resembles the way humans actually accumulate skills.

But to be clear, I see this as the right direction. For years the field has been betting that scaling up memorization would get you to general intelligence, and I've always thought that was a dead end. What's happening with O1 is the field pivoting toward search and synthesis. It's an early, somewhat crude form of it, but it's the first time I've seen a frontier lab deploy something that's structurally closer to what I think intelligence actually requires.

astra-6.text:
I think program synthesis is a natural direction for these systems, although I don’t know the internal details of O1, so I would distinguish what it might be doing from what we can actually establish.

A language model can propose candidate programs, and then you can execute those programs, evaluate the results, and use that feedback to guide further search. That’s a powerful combination: the model supplies a prior over promising solutions, while execution gives you a way to check them. You’re no longer relying entirely on generating the right answer in one pass.

But spending more computation at inference time doesn’t, by itself, mean you’re doing program synthesis. You could be searching over verbal reasoning paths. The interesting question is what representation you’re searching over and how you verify a candidate solution.

For me, the promise is in combining learned intuition with explicit search and discrete, executable representations. The learned component makes the search tractable; the search lets you construct a solution to a new problem rather than simply retrieve a familiar pattern. Of course, whether that produces genuine generalization depends on what happens when the problem requires something substantially different from what you’ve seen before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think program synthesis is a very natural direction for these systems. You can use a language model to propose a program, execute it, look at the result, and then revise it. That gives you a way to search over solutions instead of expecting a single forward pass to produce the answer.

Now, I don’t know how O1 works internally, so I wouldn’t claim that it’s doing program synthesis specifically. Longer reasoning traces could support that kind of process, but a reasoning trace isn’t necessarily an executable program, and generating more text isn’t necessarily an effective search procedure.

The interesting question is: what provides the feedback? With code, you can run tests. In mathematics, sometimes you can verify a proof. When you have a reliable way to check a candidate solution, you can spend more computation searching and actually make progress. Without that, you risk producing increasingly elaborate explanations without getting closer to a correct answer.

So I see language models as potentially very useful guides for program search. They can provide a prior over what solutions are worth trying. But the ability to propose something plausible and the ability to discover and verify a new solution are different capabilities. Combining them is where things get interesting.
